The self-care and watch framework covers mild, stable, familiar concerns where the general example shows no danger signals: everyday muscle soreness after activity in the example, a mild cold in the example, or a minor bruise in the example. The framework has two parts that must stay together: comfort measures at home, and watching with clear stop rules that move the general example to a higher framework if anything changes. body:
This Signature-original entry teaches how the care settings differ through an original door framework: Door 1 Now for emergency care, Door 2 Today for urgent same-day care, Door 3 Planned for routine appointments, and Door 4 Watch for self-care with stop rules. The door names are a Signature-original teaching design, not a clinical standard. The four frameworks differ along five general lines: speed, depth, records, tools, and purpose. Speed runs from immediate in emergency care to planned in routine care. Depth runs the other way: routine care has the longest history and the fullest picture, while emergency care has the sharpest focus on the immediate problem. Records, tools, and purpose follow the same pattern, and understanding the pattern is what lets a person match a general example to a framework without diagnosing anything.

Speed: emergency care is immediate, urgent care is same-day, routine care is booked ahead, and self-care starts at once at home.

Depth: routine care reviews the whole picture over time, urgent care answers one acute concern, and emergency care answers the immediate threat first.

Records: routine settings hold the longitudinal record, urgent settings hold the visit record, and emergency settings create a record under time pressure.

Tools: emergency settings carry resuscitation and advanced imaging, urgent settings carry basic tests and wound care, and routine settings carry planning, referral, and prevention.

Purpose: emergency care preserves life and limb in the example, urgent care resolves an acute concern today, routine care manages health over time, and self-care maintains comfort while watching.

What each setting generally does follows the same pattern: emergency teams assess and stabilise, urgent teams answer one acute concern, routine teams review and plan over time, and self-care maintains comfort while watching.

Handover is part of every job in the general example: each setting leaves the next setting, or the person, with a written summary of what was found and what happens next.

A general example of mismatch: expecting a full medication review from a single urgent visit, where the routine framework is the setting built for it.

No framework is better in general: each is the right shape for a different kind of general example.

This Signature-original entry teaches cost and time general considerations through an original door framework: Door 1 Now for emergency care, Door 2 Today for urgent same-day care, Door 3 Planned for routine appointments, and Door 4 Watch for self-care with stop rules. The door names are a Signature-original teaching design, not a clinical standard. Cost and time differ sharply across frameworks, and the general pattern is worth knowing before choosing: emergency care is the most resource-intensive, urgent care sits in the middle, routine care is usually the least costly per visit but involves waiting for a booked slot, and self-care costs the least but spends the person's own time on watching. These are general patterns, not prices, since actual costs vary by place, system, and coverage, and cost must never delay the emergency framework in a general example that fits it.

Emergency care in the general example carries the highest resource cost and the longest potential wait behind more critical cases, but it is the only framework for immediate presentations.

Urgent care in the general example usually costs more than a routine visit and less than emergency care, with same-day access traded against variable waiting time.
